summary:
Pakistan stands at ground zero of the global climate emergency. From submerged plains in Sindh to rapidly melting glaciers in the Karakoram, our communities face compounding ecological shocks. Yet ground monitoring across these vast terrains remains scarce.

We built SAR-Pulse, an interactive Earth observation platform using NASA-ISRO NISAR radar to track four critical Pakistani biomes. In the Indus Basin, dual-pol radar penetrates monsoon clouds to map active floodwaters and submerged cropland. In Quetta, interferometry tracks a city sinking at 8.7 cm/year from groundwater collapse. In Islamabad, radar polarimetry detects forest canopy loss across the Margalla National Park. At Siachen Glacier, repeat-pass coherence measures accelerated ice slip.

By combining NISAR L-band and ESA Sentinel-1 data with building footprints and population grids, SAR-Pulse turns abstract microwave physics into actionable 2050 risk forecasts. We give planners, scientists, and citizens the foresight needed to protect our land before disaster strikes.
details:
The National Crisis We Face

Pakistan is one of the most climate-vulnerable nations on Earth. Our landscapes stretch from the highest frozen peaks in the world down to the fertile plains of the Indus, yet our environmental monitoring has historically been blind to invisible or cloud-covered hazards.

What SAR-Pulse Does

SAR-Pulse is an open radar intelligence platform that monitors four vital Pakistani biomes using the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission:

1. Indus River Basin (Floods and Agriculture): During monsoon catastrophes, cloud cover blinds regular optical satellites. NISAR L-band dual-polarization penetrates dense storms, using specular reflection drops to map submerged farmlands and double-bounce scattering to isolate flooded crops.

2. Quetta Valley (Urban Groundwater Subsidence): Over-pumping in an arid basin has drained deep aquifers, compacting clay layers and causing the valley floor to plunge. Combining NISAR ascending and descending orbits, we proved the ground is moving straight down at a median rate of 8.7 cm/year, verified against European Space Agency Sentinel-1 data (r = 0.89).

3. Margalla Hills in Islamabad (Canopy Loss and Urban Sprawl): Radar microwaves penetrate deep into forest crowns. By measuring cross-polarized volume scattering, we track tree density degradation and illegal encroachment into the protected Margalla National Park.

4. Siachen Glacier (Cryosphere and Ice Flow): As temperatures rise, Himalayan glaciers surge and melt. Using 12-day repeat-pass radar coherence, we track glacier velocity and basal slip acceleration from 18 cm/day up to 44 cm/day.

How It Works

Our architecture queries the NASA Alaska Satellite Facility search API to stream spatial subsets directly from Level 2 HDF5 files without requiring multi-gigabyte downloads. We combine radar physics with 195,000 building footprints and population grids in 500 Monte Carlo simulations, projecting risk scenarios through 2050 to help planners mitigate disaster before it occurs.

Tools Used

Python (numpy, scipy, h5py, rasterio, earthaccess), FastAPI serverless backend, React, Three.js 3D visualization, and open space agency radar datasets.
